Chapter 5: Inspiration and the Spiritual Side of Creative Struggle.
Once you make showing up and working with discipline a real part of your daily life, something kind of magical starts to happen. Suddenly, those moments of inspiration—those flashes of insight and clarity—just seem to show up more often. It’s like, by committing to your work, you’re opening the door to something bigger than yourself.
A lot of people who’ve been down this road describe a feeling of being guided by something they can’t quite see. Think about the songwriter who wakes up with a melody already in their mind. Or the inventor who solves a tricky problem in their sleep. Or maybe the teacher who, right in the middle of a lesson, just finds the perfect words. These moments feel like little gifts—unexpected, but always welcome.
It’s easy to think of inspiration as some rare, mysterious event that you can’t plan for. But here’s something worth paying attention to: inspiration tends to show up for those who are ready. The more consistently you show up and put in the work, the more likely it is that inspiration will find you. In a way, just showing up is like sending an invitation out into the universe, letting it know you’re ready for whatever comes.
And this isn’t just for artists or writers. Anyone who’s following a calling—whether it’s launching a business, raising a family, or serving their community—can feel this sense of guidance. The work becomes more than just ticking off tasks; it starts to feel spiritual, like you’re part of something much bigger than yourself.
For many people, this brings a real sense of humility. Suddenly, your work doesn’t feel like it’s all about personal achievement. Instead, it feels like a way of giving something back to the world. You become a kind of vessel, channeling ideas and energy that seem to come from somewhere beyond you. There’s a responsibility that comes with that—a duty to honor the gift by simply showing up and doing the work.
And you know what? The spiritual side of creative struggle can actually be a huge source of comfort. When resistance feels overwhelming, when doubts and fears start creeping in, just knowing your work has meaning beyond yourself can give you the strength to keep moving forward. That struggle turns into a kind of devotion—a way of honoring the calling you’ve received.
Of course, there are always going to be moments of doubt. The path is hardly ever a straight line, and setbacks happen. But here’s the thing: if you stick with it, you often find that the work itself becomes a source of healing and transformation. Creating something new doesn’t just change the world—it changes you, too.
